We won $2000 at a hackathon… and then got pied in the face on stage 🥧 This weekend our team won 1st place at B@BHacks 2026 at UC Berkeley. My teammates, Aryan Achuthan , Aryan Jain , Kabilesh Yuvaraj , and I, built Open Tix. The project started from an idea we pitched, a ticketing platform designed to address the ticket scalping problem. Today, once a ticket is sold, organizers lose control over how it’s resold. With OpenTix, tickets are minted as NFTs on the XRP Ledger, which makes each ticket verifiable on-chain and allows organizers to set resale price caps and receive royalties on secondary sales. The goal was to show how programmable tickets could reduce fraud, limit extreme markups, and give organizers more control over their ticket markets. At events, tickets can be scanned with a QR code that verifies ownership directly on-chain. In 9 hours, we built a working full stack prototype using React + Vite, Node.js/Express, and MongoDB, integrating XRPL NFTs (XLS-20) with xrpl.js to mint tickets, handle purchases, and verify ownership. Big thanks to Blockchain at Berkeley and the sponsors including Ripple, Anthropic, Sui, Polymarket, and Liquid for hosting such a great event! And yes… apparently winning also means getting pied in the face on stage.

♟ Engineering Leaders & VCs Play Chess — November Edition I’m amazed to see how our community of engineering and product leaders passionate about chess keeps growing. Yesterday’s event felt like a scene from The Queen’s Gambit — intense, inspiring, and deeply engaging. Our fireside chat with Yuanling Yuan , a Woman International Master, one of the top-ranked female chess players in Canada, and Partner at SignalFire, was both insightful and energizing. Watching YY play was truly special. It was a beautiful game! A huge shout-out to Aryan Achuthan , National Master, 3-time National Champion, and 9-time California State Champion, for leading our beginner sessions and simul games. So many guests shared that they finally understand what’s happening on the board — and that they actually want to keep learning! Thank you, Yuanling Yuan and Aryan Achuthan , for making it special! It’s incredible to see how chess brings together engineering leaders uniting us through shared curiosity and the love of strategy. Thank you to everyone who came, played, shared feedback, and helped make this community stronger with every edition. Stay tuned — our December holiday chess edition will be a special one! 🎄♟ With great team: Yousuf Khan Alex Bogachek Dmitry Grudzinskiy Kamilla Matyus Ridge Ventures Orion Innovation

After dozens of demos of Edviro (YC S26) , one thing that has consistently stood out: AI wasn't what sold them. I came into our first few demos expecting it to be the main selling point. And it did matter. Schools valued the ability to automatically find energy waste, surface problems, and recommend what to do next. But the first thing they noticed was much simpler: “This is really easy to use.” It’s easy to dismiss UI when you’re building a highly technical product. But the most sophisticated system in the world is useless if the person responsible for using it has to fight through ten menus to understand what it’s saying. This is one of the most underrated advantages startups have. Incumbents can add AI features. What they struggle to do is rethink decades of product decisions, legacy infrastructure, customer-specific exceptions, and workflows users have already been trained around. A startup gets a blank sheet of paper. We can design every workflow around the person actually using it, watch where they get confused, and rebuild quickly. The AI makes the product powerful. The UI makes people want to use it.

It's inspiring to see leaders who are so invested in helping the next generation grow. I also had the chance to meet so many talented engineers, founders, researchers, and students throughout the evening. Looking forward to staying in touch and continuing those conversations. #Chess #ArtificialIntelligence #DataScience #Engineering #MachineLearning #Networking #SiliconValley #AI
